sections.h2: What is King County, Washington, and where does it sit?
sections.html:
King County is the most populous county in Washington, with Seattle as both its seat and its largest city. The 2020 census counted 2,269,675 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 2,344,939.

The Oregon Territory legislature formed the county on December 22, 1852, out of Thurston County, and Seattle became the seat on January 11, 1853. It was first named for William R. King, then vice president-elect, and in 1986 the county government amended the designation to honor Martin Luther King Jr. The county's Wikipedia entry gives a total area of 2,307 square miles, of which 2,116 is land and 191 is water.

The Cascade Range fills the eastern side, and Mount Daniel is the high point at 7,959 feet. The county borders Snohomish, Chelan, Kittitas, Pierce and Kitsap counties, includes Vashon Island and Maury Island in Puget Sound, and has about 760 lakes. Cities inside it include Seattle, Bellevue, Kent, Renton, Redmond, Kirkland, Federal Way, Auburn (partly), Sammamish, Issaquah, Enumclaw, Snoqualmie and North Bend. For a seller, that spread matters because the city and special districts a parcel falls in decide which levies appear on the bill.

sections.h2: Which King County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
Three separate King County bodies touch your bill: the Department of Assessments sets values, Treasury Operations bills and collects, and the Board of Appeals and Equalization hears valuation disputes. The Board is an independent agency and is not part of the assessor's office.

Source: King County 2026 property taxes page and the Treasury FAQ. Treasury is at 201 S. Jackson St., Suite 710, in Seattle's Pioneer Square, and the Customer Service Center on the second floor takes in-person payments on weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

sections.h2: How much did King County property taxes rise for 2026?
sections.html:
Total property taxes for the 2026 tax year come to $8.4 billion, up about $770 million, or 10%, from $7.7 billion the year before. Countywide taxable value rose about 5.4%, from $873 billion to $920 billion, so the bill grew faster than values.

The Assessor's page attributes most of the increase to voter-approved measures rather than to rising property values. King County itself receives about 20% of the money collected, which pays for services such as roads, criminal justice and public health. The rest goes to the state, cities, schools and other districts.

Measures approved by voters for 2026 include:

  • Seattle: a six-year renewal levy for families, education and preschool, plus a ten-year lid lift for election vouchers.
  • Bothell: a ten-year renewal of the Safe Streets and Sidewalks lid lift.
  • Mercer Island: a $103,160,000 general obligation bond for a new facility.
  • Seattle School District: replacement capital and education and operations levies.
  • King County: a six-year parks, recreation, trails and open space levy.

Look up your own parcel in the Assessor's eReal Property tool to see its valuation, levy rates and sale history before you set a price.

sections.h2: When are King County property taxes due, and what happens if you miss a date?
sections.html:
The first half is due April 30 and the second half October 31. If a date lands on a weekend or county holiday, payment is due the next business day. King County mails statements once a year, in mid-February, and sends nothing further unless you ask, so sign up for the text or email reminders on the Treasury site.

Miss April 30 and the whole year's tax becomes delinquent on May 1, with late charges worked out monthly on the full-year amount. You can still pay the first half plus charges before October 31. If the second half is missed, monthly charges start November 1 on that unpaid portion. The county says state law bars extensions for hardship or any other reason.

Paying by mail or in person with a check costs nothing extra. Online, the card fee is 2.35% of the charge with a $2 minimum, and an eCheck costs a flat $0.55. A lender that escrows your taxes usually pays in bulk near the deadline, and the county advises contacting the lender if the payment still shows unpaid ten days after the due date.

If you believe a tax is unlawful or excessive and want to keep the right to seek a refund in court, you must hand in a separate written statement at the time you pay, saying you are paying under protest and giving every reason.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a King County property valuation?
sections.html:
Send a petition to the King County Board of Appeals and Equalization after you receive your valuation notice. The board accepts petitions online through eAppeals or by mail with downloadable forms.

The deadline is set by state law in RCW 84.40.038: file by July 1 of the assessment year, or within 30 days of the notice, or within a period of up to 60 days if the county legislative authority has adopted one, whichever is later. Read the date printed on your notice and call the board on 206-477-3400 if it is unclear. The board can waive a late filing for good cause, such as a death or serious illness in the family or a documented postal delay.

A successful appeal is built on market evidence. Useful items include:

  • Recent sales of similar homes in your neighborhood.
  • A contractor's estimate for defects the assessor has not accounted for.
  • An independent appraisal.
  • Photos and records showing a wrong square footage, bedroom count or lot size.

The Assessor also takes petitions for a refund when a manifest error in the property description was used to set value, for example the wrong square footage. The maximum period is six years, depending on the evidence.

sections.h2: What tax relief can a King County homeowner claim?
sections.html:
King County runs a reduction program for owner-occupants who are at least 61, or retired because of a disability, and whose income falls under the state limit. Apply through TaxRelief.kingcounty.gov or call 206-296-3920. The exemption covers one residence and up to one acre, and only the unit the owner lives in qualifies in a multi-family building. Deferral of taxes is available under certain conditions.

Two other programs matter when you sell or renovate. If you add rooms, a deck or a patio to a single-family home, you may apply for a three-year exemption on the value of that improvement, but you must apply before construction is finished. Damaged or destroyed property can qualify for a lower assessed value; the Assessor's office answers questions on 206-263-2332.

sections.h2: What do you owe at closing when you sell a King County house?
sections.html:
The seller usually pays Washington's real estate excise tax, and the amount depends on the sale price. The Department of Revenue says the tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, whenever the deed is recorded, and penalties and interest start if it is not paid within a month. If the seller does not pay, the buyer becomes responsible and the tax can become a lien on the property.

The state portion is graduated. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the Department of Revenue lists 1.1% up to $551,000, 1.28% from there to $1,551,000, 2.75% to $3,051,000 and 3% above that. A local rate is added on top, so ask the King County Treasury or your closing agent for the combined figure for your city.

Also check the tax statement for non-tax charges that ride on the bill, which vary by location: surface water management, City of Seattle drainage, fire protection, King Conservation District and noxious weed fees. If a new house or addition was never assessed, an omit tax can reach back up to three years and is billed with an extra year to pay.

sections.h2: Can you sell a King County house that is behind on taxes?
sections.html:
Yes, a house with unpaid taxes can be sold, and the balance is paid from the proceeds, but the amount keeps growing until then. Call the Treasury hotline at 206-263-2890 for a current figure, and use 206-263-2649 for any parcel in foreclosure, because foreclosure costs are added and cannot be paid online.

King County offers payment plans for past due prior-year taxes. A plan runs no longer than 12 months, late charges are not reduced, there is a one-time $100 setup fee for each plan, and a vendor adds a monthly processing fee. Taxes three years or more past due can be sent to foreclosure. State law lets an income-qualified owner living in the home ask for interest and penalties to be waived shortly before that three-year mark, as described in RCW 84.56.020.

If the clock is the problem, a direct sale to a cash buyer can close before the tax situation worsens, but compare it with listing on the market and with a payment plan before you decide.

faqs.q: What is the King County property tax deadline in 2026?
faqs.a: The deadlines are April 30 for the first half and October 31 for the second half. The first half has passed, and the second half date passed on October 31, 2026, so any unpaid second half is now delinquent with monthly late charges from November 1.

faqs.q: Where do I file a King County valuation appeal?
faqs.a: File with the King County Board of Appeals and Equalization, online through eAppeals or by mail. It is separate from the Assessor, and its phone number is 206-477-3400.

faqs.q: Who pays real estate excise tax when I sell in King County?
faqs.a: The seller usually pays it, and it is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale. The state rate is graduated by price, and a local rate is added, so get the combined figure from Treasury or your closing agent.

faqs.q: Can seniors lower their King County property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Owners who live in the home and are at least 61, or retired due to disability, may qualify if income is under the state limit. Apply at TaxRelief.kingcounty.gov or call 206-296-3920.

faqs.q: Does King County offer a payment plan for back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, for past due prior-year taxes. Plans last up to 12 months, late charges still apply, and there is a one-time $100 setup fee per plan. Call 206-263-2649 or email PaymentPlans@kingcounty.gov.
